newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Asia-Pacific grain imports seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Pacific grain imports seen rising.

text.p: Rising grain imports by emerging countries in the Asia-Pacific region, led by China, are expected to drive prices higher up to the year 2000, officials and analysts said on Tuesday.

"(Studies) clearly indicate that China will lead net grain importers by developing countries in the region in the next 20 years," Robert Evenson, professor of economics at Yale University, said in an interview.

Evenson was referring to papers to be presented at a three-day forum on food and agricultural policy changes among members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) grouping that opened in Manila on Tuesday.

APEC groups some of the world's fastest growing economies and includes Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore and the United States.
Evenson said the growing prosperity of some countries in the region was increasing appetites for meat consumption, pushing up demand for feed grains.
"As income grows, the diet (also) improves from cereal grains to meat, malt and eggs," he said.
China's rising demand for more grains to feed its swelling population is expected to affect the prices of commodities world wide, analysts said.

"China will become a more important player in world grain markets as an importer in the coming decades," according to a paper presented by Jikun Huang, an economist at the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences.

"Net grain imports of 25 to 30 million tonnes are very likely the level of China's annual grain imports in the coming decade and is also a figure likely to be acceptable to Chinese government as this represents about four to five percent of domestic grain demand," he added.
"Increases in China's food imports will slightly raise world prices for wheat, maize, and drive up world prices for livestock products as well as feed grains," Huang said.
But Evenson said he expected grain prices to remain stable as countries in the region reap the fruits of more resources put into farm productivity.
"As countries realise more industrialisation, you'll get spillovers in productivity into the agricultural sector," Evenson added.
China's rising commodity imports will push up prices of basic commodities "in times of droughts and floods," said Philippine agriculture assistant secretary Marinella Castillo.
Grain exporters like North America, Argentina, Australia and New Zealand are also expected to export more.
Economists said the promotion of more free trade will eventually bring down the cost of food in the region in the next decade.
Farmers from developing member countries of APEC, however, said easy access of subsidised grains would kill small farmers.
